summary: R.O.X.Y. is an Augmented Reality system prototype designed to help the first astronauts on Mars navigate unfamiliar terrain and make informed exploration decisions. We developed a simulated helmet display that brings navigation, terrain hazards, scientific observations, and mission resources into one view, with voice controls for hands-free interaction. R.O.X.Y. combines a first-person reconstruction of Perseverance’s Skinner Ridge terrain with NASA mineral and nighttime infrared observations. Astronauts can compare routes, identify steep or uneven ground, and access relevant map layers through voice commands. Simulated oxygen and power levels, return-to-base warnings, and dust and solar-event scenarios demonstrate how changing conditions could affect an expedition. R.O.X.Y. translates complex planetary data into accessible guidance, helping astronauts maintain awareness while focusing on exploration. Our prototype demonstrates this concept in a browser simulation, clearly distinguishing measured observations, inferred terrain, and simulated conditions.
details:
You’re 140 million miles from the nearest hospital. The sun is setting over Jezero crater, your base is out of sight, and the ground between you and home has never been walked by anyone. You think you’re alone out here. You’re not. You have R.O.X.Y.

What is R.O.X.Y?

R.O.X.Y is an Augmented-Reality based helmet display for the first people to walk on Mars. It lays everything NASA knows about the ground in front of you directly over what you see: where it’s safe to step, what the rocks are made of, what the sky is about to do, and how to get home. You don’t press buttons in a pressurized glove; you just say “Roxy,” and ask.

What brings you home:

The Science at a Glance

Earlier today, R.O.X.Y helped you find the rocks worth sampling. Its thermal overlay, built on night-time infrared data from NASA’s Mars Odyssey, shows how the ground holds heat, which separates solid bedrock from loose dust. Its mineral overlay adds what orbiters have detected in the soil.

The Safest Path, Not Just the Shortest

A straight line on Mars can end at a ledge. R.O.X.Y plans every route on real terrain, measured in three dimensions by NASA’s Perseverance rover. It scores each footstep-sized patch of ground for steepness and unevenness, rules out anything too dangerous to cross, and draws the safest way through right on the surface ahead of you. Ask why it chose that route, and it tells you.

Eyes on Every Threat

Now you’re on your way home. R.O.X.Y’s overlays mark the jagged slopes you can’t see in the dark and flag incoming dust and solar storms using NASA’s space-weather records. Your oxygen, suit power and vital signs sit in the corner of your eye. The moment your reserves are only just enough to make it back, R.O.X.Y tells you, clearly, and lights the route home.

Hands-Free, Always

Every feature answers to your voice. “Roxy, map.” “Roxy, route to Olympus Mons south opening.” “Roxy, take me home.” A planning view lifts you above the terrain to see the whole walk, then drops you back into your own boots. Your hands stay free for the work you came to do.

Real Ground, Real Data

R.O.X.Y is not a game level dressed up as Mars. The terrain under your feet is Skinner Ridge in Jezero crater, rebuilt from stereo images taken by Perseverance’s navigation cameras. The thermal and mineral layers come from NASA orbiters. The storm alerts come from NASA’s space-weather database. When R.O.X.Y says a slope is too steep, it’s because a rover measured it.

The first explorers on Mars will be the most isolated humans in history, with a twenty-minute delay to anyone who could help. They need a guide that is already there with them, one that knows the ground, watches the sky and never loses the way back. That is why Renispace built R.O.X.Y.

Our Tech Stack

Our implementation of the Skinner Ridge scenario simulator in R.O.X.Y. has been created using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS. The three-dimensional model of the terrain and the HUD view is created with the use of Three.js, whereas Node.js and npm handle the local server, creation of the terrain, and automated tests. We implemented the sky and the position of the Sun on Mars using Python, SpiceyPy, and NumPy from the NASA SPICE files. Testing and navigation were done using the keyboard, mouse, and microphone inputs in Chrome under Windows.

R.O.X.Y is not just a navigation tool. It’s safety, reliability, and efficiency.
